prompt: A pipeline runs 200 tests. Each independently has a 0.5% chance of a flaky failure per run. Roughly what fraction of runs on **correct** code will be red?

options.explanation: Correct. The chance that all 200 pass is 0.995 raised to the power 200, about 0.367, so the chance that at least one flakes is about 0.633.
Too low. Even a rough linear estimate gives 200 × 0.5% = 100%, which overshoots, but the true value is far above 10%.
That's the per-test rate. A run is red if *any* of the 200 tests flakes, so the chances compound.
Adding 200 × 0.5% gives 100%, but probabilities of independent events don't add like this; you multiply the chances of passing.

workedExample:
```formula
P_red = 1 − (1 − p)^N
P_red = 1 − 0.995^200
0.995^200 = e^(200 × ln(0.995))
0.995^200 ≈ e^(−1.0025) ≈ 0.367
P_red ≈ 1 − 0.367 = 0.633
where
P_red: the probability that a run on correct code goes red, from 0 (never) to 1 (always)
p: the probability that one test flakes in one run; 0.5 % = 0.005
N: the number of tests; 200
^: raise to a power: (1 − p)^N is the chance that all N independent tests pass
e: Euler's number, about 2.718, the base of natural logarithms
ln: the natural logarithm (log to base e), which turns a power into a multiplication so it is easy to work out by hand
≈: approximately equal to
In words: a run is red unless every test passes; 200 chances of a 0.5 % flake make a red run more likely than not.
```

1. One test passes with probability 1 − 0.005 = 0.995.
2. All 200 pass with probability 0.995 raised to the power 200 (200 copies of 0.995 multiplied together).
3. Using logarithms: 200 × ln(0.995) ≈ −1.0025, and e to that power is about 0.367.
4. So a run is red with probability about 0.633.

Nearly two-thirds of runs on good code fail, so engineers stop trusting red. Cutting per-test flakiness to 0.1% leaves about 82% of runs green (0.999 to the power 200), still 18% red. This hypothetical independent-probability model illustrates compounding risk; it is not a causal derivation of Google's observed transition statistics. Flaky failures can also expose real defects.

link.title: Flaky Tests at Google and How We Mitigate Them
